correctness.rationale: Induct on appending a letter to prove B=binom(r,2)+h-t pointwise; identify i.i.d. uniform modular increments and independent nonzero-boundary Bernoulli indicators. Conditional on boundaries, adjacent inverse increments are independent Bernoulli(1/(q-1)), so t has a Binomial(J,1/(q-1)) law. Expand conditional mean into orthogonal centered square-free Bernoulli monomials; add conditional variance to recover exact formula. Handle n=2 directly; verify raw deletion sets and independent conditional moments by two standalone packages for q=2,3,4,5 on finite lengths. No finite experiment is used as an infinite proof.

originality.rationale: The public binary variance formula expressly covers only q=2, whereas the final claim is an exact uniform-input variance for every q>=3. Deterministic q-ary subsequence counts and extremal run bounds do not themselves state a distributional second moment. Direct statement/implication searches across research records and primary texts found no matching nonbinary evaluated variance. Mercier et al. 2008 remains a material-access residual risk: its deterministic analysis might contain a previously unnoticed related averaging. This is qualified best-knowledge originality, not independent certification.
residual_risks: Mercier et al. (2008) complete text was inaccessible through available authorized channels; it could contain a q-ary moment treatment not exposed in abstract.
An unindexed thesis, paper or differently formulated statistical computation could imply the exact q>=3 second moment.
Independent mathematical and historical-priority audits have not been performed.

value.rationale: Deletion-ball cardinality is a standard channel-geometry statistic governing varying numbers of distinct descendants. For nonbinary alphabets, including the four-symbol DNA case, its exact uniform-center dispersion and leading cubic coefficient provide all-length quantified nonregularity beyond maximum/minimum and first-moment results. The conditional inverse-increment decomposition is structural; the claim does not assert a coding-rate theorem or falsely inflate a small finite census.
